Asa Fitch
 
Anthropic’s IPO Is the Signal Amid the AI Noise
 
Plus, Jensen Huang’s apology, and hackers find a new target
 
 
KENT NISHIMURA/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

Change is in the air for the AI boom.

 

The elections last Tuesday tilted the balance of power in Congress to Democrats, many of whom aren’t as laissez-faire about AI as their Republican counterparts. AI-related stocks tanked on Thursday, wiping out $2.5 trillion of market value.

 

Then came Nvidia’s stunning revelation Sunday: Chief Executive Jensen Huang admitted an affair with an executive at a Singapore-based data-center company who U.S. officials believe was passing intelligence to China. The scandal cast doubt over Huang’s position as CEO of the company he’s led since the 1990s. Nvidia’s stock fell about 4% on Monday, and declined further Tuesday.

 

More news dropped from Anthropic on Tuesday. The giant AI lab is seeking a $1.33 trillion valuation in its IPO, below the $1.5 trillion investors were anticipating just a week ago. The biggest litmus test this year for the AI trade isn’t looking encouraging so far.

 

The question for investors, though, is how much of this is noise, and to what extent does it signal a more permanent shift in the AI boom?

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: PWC
 
 
We Turn AI Noise Into AI Solutions
 
Everyone is talking about AI. But is any of it actually working for your business? At PwC, we help cut through the AI noise so you can solve the problems that matter.
 
Learn More  >
 
 
 

The answer is likely that it is a bit of both.

 

There have been blips in the boom before. Early last year, a cutting-edge AI model from China’s DeepSeek raised concerns AI labs wouldn’t need as many chips to train frontier models. Nvidia’s stock plunged.

 

That reaction proved premature. DeepSeek’s advances were driven largely by copying the intelligence of the world’s cutting-edge models, and its efficiency gains didn’t dent demand for computing power. Big-tech pocketbooks stayed open, and Nvidia’s stock has risen 45% since.

 

Some of today’s concerns will likely have more of a lasting impact than others.

 

Democrats tipped to chair powerful committees in the Senate and House plan to investigate the impact of data centers on electricity prices. They also want to look into the proliferation of circular financing deals.

 

That could slow data-center development in the U. S.—as could numerous anti-data-center ballot measures voters approved last week. On another level, though, the data-center debate will have to balance concerns about electricity prices against U.S. national-security interests. Local political opposition could imperil specific data centers, but a countrywide moratorium seems far-fetched.

 

The Nvidia scandal probably won’t have much of an impact on the boom in the long run either, unless Huang has to step down. Congress is also involved there: A House panel has asked the CEO to appear later this month.

 

But in that case, too, politicians will factor in the geopolitical implications of trying to force him out, which would weaken the company and possibly even play into China’s hands. Strengthened controls on chip exports are likely, but that could actually benefit the U.S. AI ecosystem by making more chips available domestically. 

 

Anthropic’s IPO is a better place to look for signals. Weaker-than-expected demand for its shares is part of a long-brewing capital crunch for AI. Chip buyers have drained their cash, run up debt and are now trying to sell wary investors on supplying billions more dollars to fuel spending.

 

If they can’t raise that money, data centers won’t get built no matter what politicians say. That makes a successful Anthropic IPO vital.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ AI & Business newsletter, a weekly digest to help you make sense of AI’s impact on business with news, insights and data from our global team of technology journalists. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

Silicon Valley’s Data Center Hand-Wringing Begins

 
 
SHELBY TAUBER/REUTERS
 

Hostility to data centers in the U.S. has been building. Last week’s election results made clear it is a serious threat to Silicon Valley’s grand AI ambitions. Conversations about how to navigate an opposition movement that has significantly sharper teeth have grown in the tech world over the past week. Some companies are approaching governors-elect and trying to ascertain what they plan to do, although the mood overall has been gloomy. Brad Gerstner, a prominent tech investor, suggested on a podcast that 35% of U.S. data-center projects planned next year could be in jeopardy.

 
 
 

The Number

 
$7.1 Billion
 

SoftBank Group’s loss in its most recent quarter, due largely to charges on power-generation equipment for AI data-center projects in the U.S.

 
 
 

What the Humans Are Saying

 

“I owe my family and all of you an apology. There is no excuse for what I did.”

 

— Jensen Huang in an email to employees, two of whom are his own children, confessing his affair.

 
 
 

AI in Charts

 
 
 
 

Nvidia’s stock looks cheap—even cheaper since the company’s alleged spy scandal took the wind out of its shares this week.

 

Normally, a company as fast-growing as Nvidia with a forward price-to-earnings ratio near 12 would be a bargain for investors. But there is a wrinkle: Successful companies often look cheap when they are about to take a big fall.

 

The reason is simple. Investors won’t place a high value on a company’s future profits when those earnings look like they are in jeopardy. In highly cyclical industries like Nvidia’s, undervaluation near the top of the cycle is par for the course.

 

Of course, it isn’t clear in Nvidia’s case whether the divergence between its strong growth trajectory and weak valuation is justified or not. The company could prove markets wrong and keep expanding profits for longer than its valuation implies. There is, however, a big measure of doubt about the future baked into its price.

 
 
 

AI in the Wild

 
 
Angelo Saraceno, Solutions Engineer at Railway, in his home office. CLARK HODGIN FOR WSJ
 

Cybercriminals are starting to go after a new kind of digital asset: computing power. Hackers are now targeting so-called API keys—a kind of password that allows access to AI models from leading American labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. The keys allow hackers to use those models, running up charges that are billed to the companies they stole the keys from.

 
 
 

Other Highlights From the Week in AI

 

• In another sign of weakness in the IPO market, the Nvidia-backed startup Cohere says the timing of its listing is uncertain despite surging revenue.

 

• Google is expanding in Malaysia, planning to invest $15 billion in new campuses there over the next couple of years.

 

• Google parent Alphabet is also building a new manufacturing facility in Texas for its drone unit.
